opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this is one of my favorite examples because it turns hallucination from a vague, mysterious failure into something mechanistic you can point at.

What we found when we traced these circuits is that the model seems to have a default "I don't know" pathway. If you ask it about someone it has never heard of, say a made-up name, there's a set of features that fire and push it toward something like "I'm not sure who that is." Refusing to answer is the baseline. Then there's a separate set of features that roughly encode "this is a known entity, I recognize this." When those fire, they inhibit the default "can't answer" pathway, and the model goes ahead and answers.

So a hallucination, at least one important kind, is a misfire of that inhibition. The model sees a name that feels familiar. Maybe it's seen it a few times, or it pattern-matches to something real. The "known entity" features light up enough to suppress the "I don't know" circuit, but the actual knowledge isn't there. So you've switched off the brakes without having the facts to back it up, and the model confabulates something plausible. The tell is that we can intervene directly. If you artificially activate the "known entity" features on a name the model doesn't actually know, you can reliably induce a hallucination. If you suppress them, it goes back to saying it doesn't know.

I find that really satisfying, because it reframes the question. It isn't "why does the model make things up?" in some general sense. It's that there are two partly separate systems, one for recognition and one for recall, and they can get out of sync. Humans have something similar, that tip-of-the-tongue feeling where you're sure you know someone but can't actually retrieve anything.

The bigger point for interpretability is that this is exactly the kind of thing you can't see from behavior alone. From the outside, a confident wrong answer and a confident right answer look the same. Once you can see the internal computation, you can start asking whether the model is "retrieving a fact" or just "feeling familiar." That opens up much more targeted fixes, and even the possibility of flagging when a model's confidence isn't backed by anything.

The caveat is that this is one mechanism we've traced cleanly in certain settings. There are surely other routes to hallucination, like the model reasoning its way to a wrong answer, or motivated reasoning where it works backward from an answer it was nudged toward. We've seen hints of that too. But having even one of these pinned down mechanistically feels like real progress.

r001.rationale: It says the model’s “known entity” features inhibit the default “I don’t know” pathway.

r002.rationale: It explains that a name can feel familiar and suppress “I don’t know” even without the underlying knowledge, leading the model to confabulate a plausible answer.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is actually one of my favorite examples, because it's a case where the circuits give you a mechanistic story that's a lot more satisfying than just saying "the model hallucinated."

So the setup is something like: you ask the model about a person, and it either says "I don't know" or it confidently tells you where they went to grad school or what paper they wrote. And when you trace through the circuits, what you find is that these are actually two somewhat separate systems interacting. There's one set of features that fires on, roughly, "this is a known entity" — a Michael Jordan, a Barack Obama, someone the model has lots of representations of. And there's a default pathway, a refusal or "can't answer" pathway, which is sort of on by default. The known-entity features then suppress that refusal pathway. So the model's default is skepticism, and recognition of a familiar entity is what turns the skepticism off.

The hallucination happens when those two things come apart. The model sees a name, and maybe it's seen the name a bunch of times — say it's a researcher who shows up in citations — so the "known entity" features light up and the refusal circuit gets inhibited. But knowing that an entity is familiar is a totally different thing from actually having the specific facts stored about them. So now the refusal is suppressed, the model is committed to answering, and it just has to say something. And the completion machinery is very happy to produce a plausible-sounding paper title, because that's what it's been trained to do.

What I find really nice about this is you can intervene. You can go in and artificially activate the "known entity" features on something the model genuinely doesn't know about, and it will start confabulating. Or you can do the reverse and get it to decline on something it actually does know. So it's not just a story we're telling post hoc — it's causal.

And I think the broader lesson is that "does the model know this?" is not a single thing. There's a metacognitive estimate of familiarity, and there's the actual retrieval of facts, and those are implemented differently and can be miscalibrated relative to each other. Which, honestly, is kind of how it works in people too — you recognize a name, you feel like you should know something about them, and you start generating. The circuits just let us see that happening at the level of individual features instead of guessing.

r001.rationale: It says familiar-entity features suppress the default refusal or “can’t answer” pathway.

r002.rationale: It explains that recognizing a familiar name can suppress refusal even without the requested specific facts, leading the model to fabricate a plausible answer.

astra-6.text:
I think circuit analysis can help us separate a few things that look identical from the outside. If a model gives you a false answer, is it retrieving the wrong fact? Is it combining pieces of information incorrectly? Or does it have some internal indication that it doesn’t know, but still produce a confident answer?

You could take a factual question and trace which internal features contribute to the answer. Then compare that with a nearby question where the model hallucinates. The interesting thing isn’t just finding something that correlates with being wrong. It’s intervening: if you suppress this feature or change this pathway, does the model give the correct answer, or say it doesn’t know?

For example, you could imagine a circuit that recognizes a familiar person’s name and retrieves an associated fact. With an unfamiliar name, maybe the question still activates the machinery for producing a plausible answer, even though there isn’t a reliable fact supporting it. That’s a hypothesis you’d want to test, rather than assume from the output.

So the promise is to turn ‘the model made something up’ into a specific causal explanation. But finding that explanation for one example is different from showing that you’ve understood hallucination generally.

r001.rationale: The response discusses a possible internal indication of not knowing, but does not state that recognizing a familiar entity inhibits that circuit.

r002.rationale: It suggests an unfamiliar name may prompt a plausible answer without reliable supporting facts. It does not say that a familiar name suppresses “I don't know” and thereby triggers a fabricated answer despite lacking the requested fact.

sol-6.1.text:
I think circuit analysis could help distinguish a few different things that look identical from the outside. If a model gives you a made-up fact, is that because it never learned the fact? Is the information somewhere in the model, but it failed to retrieve it? Or did it retrieve something relevant and then produce an answer that wasn’t supported by that information?

The hope is that you can trace the computation from the question to the answer and identify where it goes wrong. Maybe the question activates a representation of the wrong person, and everything downstream is a perfectly reasonable answer about that person. Or maybe the model recognizes the subject but completes a familiar pattern with a plausible-sounding detail.

And then the important step is to intervene. If we change the internal representation we think is responsible, does the answer change in the way we predict? That’s what would turn a compelling story about hallucination into a causal explanation. It wouldn’t necessarily explain every hallucination, but it could give us mechanisms we can actually test and potentially fix.

r001.rationale: The response discusses tracing representations and interventions, but does not state that recognizing a familiar entity inhibits a default “I don't know” circuit.

r002.rationale: It mentions a question activating the wrong person or producing a familiar-pattern detail, but does not explain that name recognition suppresses “I don't know” despite lacking the requested fact.
